paragraphs: Finding good solutions to difficult graph optimization problems creates a tradeoff between speed and solution quality. Handcrafted heuristics can work quickly, while learning a complete solution directly can place heavy demands on a model. This paper proposes dividing the work between a learned component and an existing heuristic solver.

The framework has two levels. At the upper level, a learning method changes the graph, for example by adding, removing, or modifying edges. At the lower level, a heuristic solves the problem on that modified graph. Learning therefore focuses on preparing a useful graph for the solver rather than producing the entire solution itself.

This division simplifies the learning task and can reduce the model capacity it requires. Experiments cover directed acyclic graph scheduling, graph edit distance, and the Hamiltonian cycle problem. The reported results show advantages over manually designed heuristics and methods that learn solutions in a single stage, supporting the usefulness of combining learned graph modifications with established solving procedures.
neurips-2021-a-bi-level-framework-for-le.tldr: A two-level framework learns to modify graphs so that a heuristic solver can find better solutions.

paragraphs: Many decision systems first predict unknown quantities and then use those predictions in an optimization problem. Training the predictor to reduce prediction error can be misaligned with the quality of the resulting decision. Decision-focused learning addresses this mismatch, but the abstract identifies soft constraints involving a maximum operation as an obstacle for existing approaches.

The paper develops a surrogate objective that can be differentiated analytically. Its scope includes linear programming and semi-definite negative quadratic programming with soft linear constraints and non-negative hard constraints. The framework establishes bounds on constraint multipliers and derives a closed-form solution in terms of predictive parameters, making gradients available for variables in the problem.

These gradients connect predictor training to the downstream objective even when soft constraints are present. Evaluations use synthetic linear programming, portfolio optimization, and resource provisioning, each extended to include such constraints. The reported improvements over traditional two-stage training and other decision-focused methods support the framework’s value for the optimization settings studied.
neurips-2021-a-surrogate-objective-frame.tldr: An analytically differentiable surrogate connects prediction training to optimization objectives that include soft constraints.

paragraphs: Explaining a trained neural network after the fact is different from designing an architecture whose mathematical form supports interpretation. CoFrNets pursue the latter approach. Their structure is inspired by continued fractions, which have useful approximation properties in number theory. The paper investigates whether that structure can support both expressive prediction and understandable models.

The authors show how CoFrNets can be trained efficiently and interpreted through their functional form. They also prove universal approximation, using a proof strategy different from the usual arguments based on unlimited network width or depth. This result establishes representational capability; the experiments separately examine how the architecture performs and what can be extracted from it.

On nonlinear synthetic functions, CoFrNets accurately model the functions and estimate feature contributions, including higher-order terms in some cases. Across seven real datasets covering tabular, text, and image inputs, their performance is comparable to or significantly better than other interpretable models and multilayer perceptrons. Some results approach the accuracy of state-of-the-art models.
neurips-2021-cofrnets-interpretable-neur.tldr: CoFrNets use a continued-fraction-inspired architecture to combine expressive prediction with interpretation through the model’s functional form.

paragraphs: A generative adversarial network learns through competition between a generator and a discriminator. With little training data, the discriminator can overfit, obstructing the generator’s convergence. This paper targets that imbalance with Adaptive Pseudo Augmentation, or APA, a strategy that uses the generator’s own images to change what the discriminator encounters during training.

APA augments the real-data distribution with generated images and adaptively deceives the discriminator. Its central idea is to use the model’s current synthetic output to help maintain productive competition between the two components. This provides an alternative to approaches centered on standard data augmentation or regularizing the model.

The authors report extensive experiments showing improved image synthesis quality when data are limited. They also provide a theoretical analysis of the strategy’s rationale and convergence. APA can be incorporated into contemporary GANs such as StyleGAN2 with negligible computational cost, according to the abstract. The contribution is therefore both a training mechanism for reducing discriminator overfitting and a lightweight way to apply that mechanism.
neurips-2021-deceive-d-adaptive-pseudo-a.tldr: Adaptive Pseudo Augmentation uses generated images to reduce discriminator overfitting and improve GAN training with limited data.

paragraphs: Allocating jobs fairly becomes more complicated when the jobs must also fit into feasible schedules. This paper studies jobs assigned to heterogeneous machines controlled by agents. Each job has a release time, a deadline, and a processing duration, and its entire execution must fit inside that permitted time window.

The allocation must respect two different kinds of requirements. Jobs on the same machine cannot overlap, while different machines can receive different utility from processing the same job. As a result, dividing jobs fairly requires attention to both what each agent values and which combinations of jobs its machine can actually process.

The authors study maximin share fairness and envy-freeness as two criteria for evaluating allocations. For each criterion, they investigate how far fair allocations can be guaranteed and give constant approximation algorithms in various settings. These results connect fairness questions to scheduling constraints: the contribution concerns both the existence of suitable allocations and algorithmic ways to approximate fairness when allocating time-dependent work.
neurips-2021-fair-scheduling-for-time-de.tldr: The paper studies fair job allocation under scheduling constraints and develops constant approximation algorithms for several settings.

paragraphs: Speech recognition output can be improved by a second model that corrects its text. Producing corrections one token at a time adds substantial latency, while straightforward parallel generation can sacrifice accuracy. FastCorrect addresses this tradeoff by organizing parallel correction around the insertion, deletion, and substitution patterns found in recognition errors.

During training, edit distance provides an alignment between a recognized sentence and its correct version. From that alignment, FastCorrect extracts how many target tokens correspond to each source token. It trains a length predictor on those counts and adjusts the source sequence to the target length, providing a structure for generating corrected tokens in parallel.

At inference time, predicted token counts perform that adjustment without access to the correct sentence. Tests on AISHELL-1 and an internal industrial-scale dataset report inference six to nine times faster than autoregressive correction while maintaining correction accuracy, with an eight to fourteen percent word error rate reduction. FastCorrect also substantially outperforms the tested non-autoregressive models adapted from translation and text editing.
neurips-2021-fastcorrect-fast-error-corr.tldr: FastCorrect uses edit alignment and token-count prediction to correct speech recognition output efficiently through parallel generation.

paragraphs: Learning new concepts sequentially can cause a neural network to lose competence on concepts it learned earlier. This paper addresses that continual-learning problem through meta-learning: it trains a model to acquire a way of learning that supports continued adaptation. The aim is to use prior experience efficiently while preserving previously acquired concepts.

Inspired by human concept learning, the authors develop a generative classifier that uses data-driven experience to learn new concepts from few examples. They describe the proposed method as immune to forgetting and able to retain all previous concepts. The architectural choice places generative classification at the center of their approach to continual learning.

The paper supports the method with cognitive and theoretical insights alongside extensive experiments on standard benchmarks. It reports effective learning and retention with negligible computational and structural overhead. Together, these findings suggest that generative models offer a useful route for alleviating catastrophic forgetting. That broader implication is presented as a direction supported by the proposed method, rather than a guarantee about every generative model.
neurips-2021-generative-vs-discriminativ.tldr: A meta-learned generative classifier learns new concepts from few examples while retaining previous concepts with negligible overhead.

paragraphs: Hierarchical reinforcement learning can divide a difficult task between a higher level that chooses subgoals and a lower level that carries them out. However, a destination alone may be inadequate when parts of the environment change beyond the agent’s immediate control. In those settings, reaching a state at the right time also matters.

HiTS adds timing to the communication between levels. The higher level specifies both the desired goal state and when the lower level should reach it. This allows the agent to adapt its behavior to environmental dynamics. The paper also discusses why communicating through timed subgoals makes the higher level’s learning problem more stable.

The authors evaluate HiTS on standard benchmarks and three new challenging dynamic environments. They report sample-efficient learning in settings where an existing state-of-the-art subgoal-based method fails to learn stable solutions. These findings support explicitly representing time in hierarchical goals, especially for the tested problems where environmental changes make the timing of an action consequential.
neurips-2021-hierarchical-reinforcement-.tldr: HiTS assigns subgoals with target times to help hierarchical agents learn stable behavior in dynamic environments.

paragraphs: This paper studies the theoretical accuracy of support vector machines built from sparse combinations of multiple kernels. The central question is how reliably such classifiers learn as the amount of data grows, and how that reliability depends on the complexity and sparsity of their representation. The contribution consists of mathematical guarantees about learning.

The authors analyze a Lasso-type regularized learning procedure in composite multi-kernel spaces. They derive both estimation bounds and upper bounds on excess risk, addressing how closely the learned model approaches its target and how much additional predictive risk remains. Their oracle convergence rates depend on kernel complexity, sparsity, sample size, and a Bernstein condition.

Those dependencies matter because the guarantees reflect more than the number of available examples: they also account for structure in the learning problem. The paper reports substantially improved rates over previous results, including additive and linear cases. Its unified analysis covers multi-kernel SVMs while contributing to the theory of high-dimensional nonparametric classification.
neurips-2021-improved-learning-rates-of-.tldr: The paper derives improved convergence guarantees for sparse multi-kernel SVMs under conditions involving complexity, sparsity, and sample size.

paragraphs: A model trained to minimize error on its training data can struggle when the test distribution changes. Invariant learning seeks relationships that remain stable across environments, but many methods require knowing which environment produced each example. That requirement is difficult to satisfy when a dataset mixes several sources without identifying them.

Kernelized Heterogeneous Risk Minimization, or KerHRM, addresses the missing-source-label setting. It combines exploration of hidden differences within the data with learning invariant relationships, performing both in kernel space. The method then feeds the resulting information back to the original neural network by specifying an invariant direction for its gradient updates.

This links two tasks that would otherwise be difficult to separate: uncovering latent environmental structure and identifying relationships that can survive distribution shifts. The authors provide theoretical justification and extensive experiments supporting the algorithm’s effectiveness. The paper’s contribution is an integrated approach to invariant learning when explicit environment labels are unavailable, with the kernel-space analysis directly influencing neural-network training.
neurips-2021-integrated-latent-heterogen.tldr: KerHRM jointly explores hidden data heterogeneity and learns invariances to guide neural-network training without explicit source labels.

paragraphs: In iterative machine teaching, a teacher supplies training examples sequentially while taking the learner’s current state into account. Previous approaches can make this expensive by searching the entire example pool at every iteration. This paper asks whether the teacher can guide learning effectively without repeatedly performing that costly input-selection step.

The proposed framework randomly chooses an input example and then synthesizes an appropriate output for it. For an image input, that output could be a label. The teacher’s effort therefore shifts from finding a particular example to designing what the selected example should teach the current learner. The paper introduces several algorithms within this framework.

The authors prove that label synthesis can retain exponential teachability while avoiding the expensive example-selection procedure. They also report empirical evidence of the framework’s value. The result makes the teaching signal itself an important object of design: adapting the output can provide strong teaching capability even when the input is selected randomly rather than through a full search.
neurips-2021-iterative-teaching-by-label.tldr: Synthesizing labels for randomly selected inputs can avoid costly teaching-example searches while retaining provable exponential teachability.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes least-squares learning in a noiseless setting where an optimal predictor exactly matches the outputs. The predictor is linear in a feature representation, but that representation may be nonlinear in the input and even infinite-dimensional. The study focuses on stochastic gradient descent with a constant step size.

The estimator of interest is the final parameter vector produced by SGD. The authors explicitly establish convergence for an example of a problem that is not strongly convex, whereas usual results rely on some form of averaging across iterates. This addresses whether the final iterate itself can have a rigorous convergence guarantee in the stated setting.

From the statistical side, the paper gives finite-time convergence rates for overparameterized learning. A detailed parameterization of the problem reveals polynomial rates that can be faster than one divided by the number of iterations. It also connects the analysis to reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. These results depend on the noiseless interpolation setup and illuminate both optimization behavior and statistical accuracy within it.
neurips-2021-last-iterate-convergence-of.tldr: For noiseless interpolating least squares, the paper proves last-iterate convergence of constant-step SGD and derives potentially faster-than-1/T rates.

paragraphs: A trustworthiness predictor tries to distinguish a classifier’s correct answers from its mistakes. This becomes difficult on large, complex image datasets, where correct predictions usually outnumber incorrect ones. The paper observes that predictors trained with several existing losses tend to label both groups as trustworthy, weakening their usefulness for recognizing errors.

The authors identify both class imbalance and difficulty separating the two groups as causes. Their proposed steep slope loss uses two opposing slide-shaped curves to separate features associated with correct predictions from those associated with incorrect predictions. The training objective is designed to improve how well this distinction generalizes beyond the examples used to learn it.

The loss is evaluated using Vision Transformer and ResNet models as trustworthiness predictors, with extensive experiments and analysis on ImageNet. The reported results show improved generalizability. Here, trustworthiness has a specific meaning: whether a classifier’s prediction is correct. The contribution is a loss function that helps learn that distinction in the large-scale setting examined.
neurips-2021-learning-to-predict-trustwo.tldr: Steep slope loss improves learning to distinguish correct classifier predictions from mistakes on large-scale image data.

paragraphs: Point-cloud detectors can lose accuracy when deployed in a different physical environment or with a different LiDAR configuration. These changes alter the geometry of the input. This paper studies adaptation from a labeled source domain to a target domain without target labels, seeking features that remain useful across that shift.

3D Contrastive Co-training, or 3D-CoCo, builds on the observation that bird’s-eye-view features transfer better than low-level geometric features. It uses separate 3D encoders with domain-specific parameters and a transformation module that learns domain-invariant bird’s-eye-view features. This lets the architecture accommodate domain-specific geometry while developing a shared representation.

The method also addresses a mismatch between the feature distribution implied by pseudo-labels and the true distribution, which hinders contrastive instance alignment. Carefully designed point-cloud transformations incorporate geometry priors to greatly reduce this mismatch. The authors construct adaptation benchmarks from three large 3D datasets and report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods, supporting the combined architecture and alignment strategy.
neurips-2021-learning-transferable-featu.tldr: 3D-CoCo combines domain-specific encoders, transferable bird’s-eye-view features, and geometry-aware transformations to adapt point-cloud detection without target labels.

paragraphs: Generalization error can exhibit double or triple descent, producing more complicated behavior than a single improvement followed by deterioration. Such patterns can also appear as training progresses. This paper investigates those dynamics in the random feature model, studying the entire evolution of training and generalization errors under gradient flow.

The authors derive an analytical description of both errors over time in the limit of large system size. Their techniques combine complex integral representations with random matrix methods based on linear pencils. The result extends the analysis beyond a final trained model to the full trajectory through which its errors develop.

Having that trajectory makes it possible to examine how double and triple descents emerge, whether and when early stopping is useful, and what descent structures occur along the time axis. The scope is the asymptotic random feature setting analyzed in the paper. Within that setting, the work offers a precise mathematical view of how training duration interacts with error behavior.
neurips-2021-model-sample-and-epoch-wise.tldr: An analytical solution tracks random-feature training and generalization errors over time, revealing descent patterns and possible opportunities for early stopping.

paragraphs: NeRV represents a video through a neural network that maps a frame index to a complete RGB image. Encoding means fitting the network to the video’s frames, and decoding means evaluating that network at the requested index. The video is therefore represented by a learned function that can reconstruct its frames.

Producing an entire image at once is central to the approach. Compared with pixel-wise implicit representations, the paper reports encoding speed improvements of 25 to 70 times and decoding improvements of 38 to 132 times, alongside better video quality. These comparisons support the efficiency of using an image-wise representation for the tested videos.

Treating a video as a network also makes network compression a way to compress the video itself. The authors report performance comparable to traditional frame-based approaches such as H.264 and HEVC. They additionally demonstrate video denoising, showing that the representation can support more than compression. The common mechanism is to perform video-related operations through the network representing its frames.
neurips-2021-nerv-neural-representations.tldr: NeRV encodes a video as a neural network that generates whole frames from their indices, enabling efficient reconstruction, compression, and denoising.

paragraphs: Batch normalization and weight decay are commonly used together when training neural networks. This paper shows that their interaction may produce a recurring pattern in optimization: training becomes destabilized, then enters another period of training. The observed behavior is periodic rather than a single disturbance followed by complete divergence.

The authors investigate the mechanism through both empirical evidence and theoretical analysis. They also examine the conditions under which the pattern appears in practice. The qualification matters: the finding is that this combination can create periodic dynamics, not that every network using these two techniques must exhibit the same training trajectory.

The paper connects the pattern to two previously opposing views of training with batch normalization and weight decay: an equilibrium perspective and an instability perspective. Periodic behavior can generalize both by placing destabilization and renewed training within one recurring process. This reframes how the interaction is understood, showing why apparent stability and instability can belong to a broader account of optimization dynamics.
neurips-2021-on-the-periodic-behavior-of.tldr: Batch normalization and weight decay can jointly produce recurring training destabilizations that connect equilibrium and instability perspectives.

paragraphs: A model given both images and text may obtain accurate answers without relying strongly on the images. Biases in large multimodal datasets can make textual shortcuts effective, even when the task is intended to require visual understanding. This paper introduces the perceptual score to quantify how much a model relies on different input modalities.

The score assesses dependence on subsets of input features, allowing the authors to examine whether visual information contributes to a model’s behavior. It can also be decomposed into contributions from subsets of the data. That decomposition helps investigate where particular patterns of reliance and bias occur within a dataset.

Across four popular datasets for visual question answering or visual dialog, the authors find a consistent trend: newer, more accurate state-of-the-art models tend to rely less on visual data than their predecessors. The finding shows why overall accuracy alone can obscure changes in how a multimodal model uses its inputs. The proposed metric provides an additional way to examine that behavior.
neurips-2021-perceptual-score-what-data-.tldr: The perceptual score measures modality reliance and reveals that higher multimodal accuracy can accompany reduced use of visual information.

paragraphs: Learning a ranking model involves a mismatch between the desired evaluation metric and the objective used for training. Ranking metrics usually depend on sorting, which is not differentiable with respect to model parameters. Existing substitutes can be only loosely connected to those metrics or difficult to apply to realistically large lists.

PiRank constructs differentiable surrogate objectives using a continuous approximation to sorting based on NeuralSort. A temperature parameter controls the relaxation. The authors show that the desired ranking metrics are recovered exactly in the limit as temperature approaches zero, providing a precise connection between the trainable objective and the evaluation target.

To handle larger lists, the paper introduces a divide-and-conquer extension with favorable scaling in both theory and practice. Experiments on public Internet-scale ranking benchmarks investigate the role of larger training lists and report significant improvements over comparable approaches. The contribution combines closer alignment with ranking metrics and a method for making that alignment practical at larger list sizes.
neurips-2021-pirank-scalable-learning-to.tldr: PiRank uses differentiable sorting to align training with ranking metrics and scales to large lists through divide-and-conquer.

paragraphs: Transformers need a useful notion of position, but graph nodes do not have the straightforward ordering of sequence elements. The Spectral Attention Network, or SAN, addresses this by learning positional information from a graph’s Laplacian spectrum. Those learned encodings are added to node features before a fully connected Transformer processes them.

The positional encoding can use the full spectrum, giving the model theoretical power to distinguish graphs and helping it recognize similar substructures through their resonance. Full connectivity also addresses over-squashing, the information bottleneck identified in many graph neural networks. The paper connects this design to better modeling of physical phenomena such as heat transfer and electrical interaction.

Across four standard datasets, SAN performs comparably to or better than state-of-the-art graph neural networks and substantially outperforms the attention-based models in the evaluation. The results support combining spectral position information with fully connected attention. In the authors’ account, this provides a successful way to bring a fully connected architecture to graph benchmarks.
neurips-2021-rethinking-graph-transforme.tldr: SAN combines learned spectral node positions with fully connected attention to improve graph representation and benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Language grounding research often evaluates models in a single environment, making it difficult to tell whether an improvement applies more broadly. SILG brings several grounded language-learning environments under a shared interface. Its purpose is to test methods across different observations, actions, language requirements, and planning challenges.

The collection includes grid worlds requiring adaptation to new entities, dynamics, and partial observations, alongside symbolic versions of visually grounded environments with complex scenes. The authors also introduce a shared reinforcement-learning architecture and evaluate components including local egocentric convolution, recurrent state tracking, entity-focused attention, and pretrained language models.

The shared architecture reaches performance comparable to architectures designed for individual environments. However, many modeling advances show no significant gains beyond the environment for which they were developed. Even the best models remain substantially below human performance. These findings make the benchmark useful for distinguishing broadly effective language-grounding methods from improvements that depend heavily on one particular environment.
neurips-2021-silg-the-multi-domain-symbo.tldr: SILG evaluates language grounding across diverse environments and finds that many environment-specific modeling gains do not transfer broadly.

paragraphs: Recovering an image from degraded measurements can leave several plausible explanations for the same observation. SNIPS approaches this uncertainty by drawing samples from the posterior distribution of a linear inverse problem. Its stated observation model assumes additive white Gaussian noise, defining the noise setting in which the method operates.

The algorithm combines ideas from Langevin dynamics and Newton’s method with a pretrained Gaussian denoiser designed for minimum mean squared error. Its derivation uses a singular value decomposition of the degradation operator to obtain a tractable posterior score and an iterative sampling procedure. These ingredients turn the restoration task into a process that can generate multiple reconstructions.

The paper demonstrates the approach on image deblurring, super-resolution, and compressive sensing. It reports sharp, detailed samples that remain consistent with the measurements. Their differences are meaningful: multiple outputs for one observation expose uncertainty inherent in the inverse problem. Thus, the method aims to provide both perceptually convincing reconstructions and a view of the range of plausible solutions.
neurips-2021-snips-solving-noisy-inverse.tldr: SNIPS samples plausible reconstructions for linear inverse problems with Gaussian noise, exposing uncertainty through diverse measurement-consistent outputs.

paragraphs: Supervised learning often optimizes a convenient surrogate loss instead of the target loss that defines success. A surrogate regret bound describes how excess error on that training objective translates into excess error on the target task. This paper develops general results about that translation for different kinds of surrogate functions.

The first result gives a linear regret bound for polyhedral surrogates, whose functions are convex and piecewise linear. A linear relationship means that rates of improvement in surrogate generalization transfer directly to target rates. This provides a broad connection between the geometry of the training loss and the guarantees available for the actual task.

The second result concerns sufficiently non-polyhedral surrogates, for which the regret relationship is a square root. In that case, fast surrogate rates translate into slower target rates. Together, the results suggest that polyhedral surrogates are optimal in many cases. The conclusion concerns how guarantees transfer between objectives, with the non-polyhedral result explicitly restricted to the sufficiently non-polyhedral class.
neurips-2021-surrogate-regret-bounds-for.tldr: Polyhedral surrogates admit linear regret transfer, while sufficiently non-polyhedral surrogates incur a square-root relationship that slows target rates.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate visually impressive images, but this paper asks whether they can also assign strong likelihoods to image data. It introduces a family of models that jointly optimizes the noise schedule and the rest of the model, linking improved density estimation to a clearer mathematical understanding of diffusion training.

The authors simplify the variational lower bound using the signal-to-noise ratio of diffused data and establish equivalences between several existing models. They show that, in continuous time, the bound depends on the noise schedule only through its endpoint signal-to-noise ratios. This permits learning the schedule to reduce the estimator’s variance, which leads to faster optimization.

Combined with architectural changes, these advances produce state-of-the-art likelihoods on standard image density estimation benchmarks, outperforming autoregressive models and often optimizing significantly faster. The paper also demonstrates a bits-back lossless compression scheme with rates close to the theoretical optimum. These results connect the theoretical analysis to both density estimation performance and a concrete compression application.
neurips-2021-variational-diffusion-model.tldr: Variational diffusion models use signal-to-noise analysis and learned noise schedules to improve likelihood estimation, optimization, and lossless compression.

paragraphs: A representation learned through self-supervised contrastive training may lose adversarial robustness when adapted to a supervised task. The paper attributes this difficulty to the mismatch between pretraining and finetuning objectives and studies how robustness can transfer across that change. Its proposed framework, AdvCL, modifies adversarial contrastive pretraining to address the problem.

Two design findings guide the method. First, the choice of contrastive views matters, and high-frequency image components are beneficial for robustness. Second, adding pseudo-supervision, such as signals obtained through feature clustering, helps retain robustness. AdvCL brings these ideas together to make the pretrained representation better suited to robust downstream adaptation.

Experiments cover CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and STL-10, using both linear evaluation and full-model finetuning. The authors report stronger robustness transfer without sacrificing model accuracy or finetuning efficiency, and improvements over state-of-the-art self-supervised robust learning methods. The findings support coordinating pretraining design with the later supervised task, rather than assuming robustness will automatically survive the transition.
neurips-2021-when-does-contrastive-learn.tldr: AdvCL uses high-frequency image information and pseudo-supervision to improve adversarial robustness transfer from contrastive pretraining to finetuning.
